newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say all refugees gone home to Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say all refugees gone home to Rwanda.

text.p: Large movements of wandering people were reported in eastern Zaire on Friday as countries backing a U.N. force prepared to meet in Germany to discuss whether military intervention was still needed.
Zairean rebels, backed by Rwanda, declared the refugee crisis was over and there was no need for any U.N.-led force.
They said satellite pictures of people on the move were either refugees closely linked with Hutu militias and former Rwandan army soldiers or thousands of internally displaced Zaireans.
"We don't see any need for a military intervention force to come to Zaire, all the refugees have gone to Rwanda, the refugee crisis is resolved," top rebel commander Andre Kassesse told reporters.
Ray Wilkinson, spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR in Goma, said hundreds of thousands of people were on the road south of Lake Kivu in the Bukavu region.

But he said the information was based on satellite imagery and that the UNHCR had no pictures from before the crisis began to compare "these figures with" and had no way of telling exactly who these people were.

Kassesse said fighters of the hardline Interahamwe militia and soldiers from the defeated Hutu army, accused of leading the 1994 Rwandan genocide, had taken to the Masisi hills west of Goma, but said no heavy fighting was currently under way.
"There are only small actions, do the international community want to come and help the Interahamwe?," he asked.

Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated government, bitter over the international community's long support of the previous hardline Hutu government and failure to act to stop the genocide, has long opposed any outside intervention.

In 1994, when hundreds of thousands of Hutus fled Rwanda fearing reprisals for the slaughter of at least 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus, Rwanda says an international intervention simply allowed the defeated gunmen to plot a comeback.

Several countries appear to have some sympathy with the Rwandan argument that many of the people currently at large in war-racked eastern Zaire are in fact Zaireans and the reason for sending a U.N. force has been largely overtaken by events.
Some countries, including the United States, scaled down their commitment after 500,000 refugees returned home to Rwanda.
Renewed fighting, with refugees caught in the middle, might however give fresh impetus to the Canadian-led mission.
The Friday meeting of military planners will not make any decisions on whether to send a force but a decision would come soon, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Thursday.
"There will not be a decision in Stuttgart. It is a meeting to look at all the factors and all the options, and after that there will be a context for a decision," Axworthy said.
Wilkinson said in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi on Thursday that UNHCR had reports of heavy fighting in Zaire, south of Minova on Lake Kivu, 20 km (12 miles) south of Sake.
"This appears to confirm the reports we've had for the past four days of a large movement of refugees and Interahamwe from south Kivu towards Sake and the north," he told reporters.
Zairean rebels ousted the Interahamwe and troops of the former Rwandan army along with refugees from camps in eastern Zaire in fighting that started in mid-October.
Some 500,000 have returned en masse to Rwanda from the Goma area, near Sake, over the past week to escape the new fighting. But the whereabouts of another 700,000 has been uncertain.

Wilkinson said aid workers would have to contend with "an ongoing diaspora" with people heading in all directions. That seemed to be confirmed with the findings of satellite photos reported by the UNHCR in Geneva on Thursday.
The United States on Thursday suspended flights of unarmed military reconnaissance planes over Zaire after one came under anti-aircraft fire on Wednesday. It was not hit.

Zaire's radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi told Radio France International on Friday that his arch foe President Mobutu Sese Seko had given him a mandate to form a national unity government.

He said after talks late on Thursday with Mobutu, who is in southern France recuperating from cancer surgery, that dialogue was the only way to end the revolt in the east and rebel leader Laurent Kabila should have a role in Zaire.
